20 Spooky Short Stories to Teach in October

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:08
Instaread

There is something about October that makes spooky short stories especially fun to teach. Maybe it’s the darker mornings, Halloween decorations popping up everywhere, or simply the fact that students are usually a little more willing to read something creepy this time of year.

But I also love spooky short stories because they give us so many opportunities to teach important literary analysis skills.

Suspense, symbolism, foreshadowing, unreliable narrators, irony, mood, point of view, characterization, and setting are practically built into the genre. And because short stories can usually be read and analyzed within a class period or two, they are an easy way to add something seasonal to your secondary ELA classroom without abandoning your curriculum.

If you’re looking for something creepy to read with your middle or high school students this October, here are 20 spooky short stories to consider, along with the literary element I’d focus on with each one.

1. “The Feather Pillow” by Horacio Quiroga

Teach: Foreshadowing

If you want a story with an ending students will remember, “The Feather Pillow” belongs on your October reading list. Throughout the story, Quiroga plants subtle clues about Alicia’s mysterious illness before revealing its horrifying cause.

Have students collect suspicious details as they read and determine which ones function as foreshadowing. After the reveal, go back and reread some of those passages. This is a great opportunity to show students how an author can prepare readers for an ending without giving it away.

2. “The Tell-Tale Heart” by Edgar Allan Poe

Teach: Unreliable Narrator

“The Tell-Tale Heart” is an October classic for a reason. Poe’s narrator insists on his sanity while simultaneously giving readers plenty of reasons to question him.

Rather than simply asking students whether the narrator is reliable, have them identify the specific details that undermine his credibility. Students can examine his word choice, behavior, contradictions, and perception of events to determine how Poe uses point of view to manipulate the reader.

3. “Where Is Here?” by Joyce Carol Oates

Teach: Setting and Ambiguity

This story takes an ordinary suburban home and slowly makes it feel deeply unsettling.

It works particularly well for examining how authors create mood through setting. Students can track the details that make the familiar setting increasingly uncomfortable and discuss the questions Oates deliberately leaves unanswered.

This is also a good story for teaching students that ambiguity can be intentional. Not every question a story raises needs to be neatly answered.

4. “Spunk” by Zora Neale Hurston

Teach: Characterization and Supernatural Elements

“Spunk” brings folklore, superstition, jealousy, fear, and revenge together in a story that works particularly well during October.

Students can examine how Hurston characterizes Spunk and Joe through dialogue, community gossip, actions, and reactions. The supernatural elements also create an interesting discussion: What does the black bobcat represent, and how does Hurston use folklore and superstition to develop the story’s conflict?

5. “The Landlady” by Roald Dahl

Teach: Foreshadowing and Dramatic Irony

“The Landlady” is one of those stories where students often realize something is wrong before the protagonist does.

That makes it perfect for teaching foreshadowing and dramatic irony. Ask students to collect the clues Dahl gives readers about the landlady and her boarding house. Then have them determine at what point they became suspicious and what Billy fails to recognize.

6. “The Monkey’s Paw” by W. W. Jacobs

Teach: Foreshadowing and Mood

“The Monkey’s Paw” gives students plenty to analyze before anything truly horrifying happens.

Students can track the warnings surrounding the paw, the reactions of the characters, the setting, and the increasingly ominous mood. It is also a natural story for discussing cause and effect because each wish creates consequences the characters did not anticipate.

7. “The Yellow Wallpaper” by Charlotte Perkins Gilman

Teach: Symbolism

The wallpaper is much more than part of the setting in this story.

Students can trace how the narrator’s perception of the wallpaper changes and analyze what it comes to represent. The story also provides opportunities to discuss characterization, point of view, and how social and historical context can deepen literary analysis.

Because of its length and subject matter, I’d generally reserve this one for older high school students.

8. “The Wife’s Story” by Ursula K. Le Guin

Teach: Point of View

This is a fantastic story for showing students just how much point of view controls a reader’s understanding.

Le Guin carefully gives readers information through the narrator’s perspective, allowing our own assumptions to fill in the gaps. Once students reach the reveal, have them go back and identify details they interpreted differently the first time.

It’s an excellent example of why close reading sometimes means rereading.

9. “The Masque of the Red Death” by Edgar Allan Poe

Teach: Symbolism

If I were choosing one Poe story specifically for symbolism, this would be it.

The seven rooms, their colors, the ebony clock, and the mysterious masked figure give students plenty to analyze. Rather than immediately telling students what each symbol represents, have them look for patterns and use textual evidence to develop their interpretations.

The story also opens up discussion about whether wealth or status can protect people from forces beyond their control.

10. “The Lottery” by Shirley Jackson

Teach: Irony

Jackson begins with an almost idyllic community gathering and slowly reveals something much darker.

Students can examine the contrast between the pleasant setting, casual behavior of the townspeople, and the eventual purpose of the lottery. It’s also an excellent story for discussing tradition, conformity, and how authors use ordinary details to make disturbing events even more unsettling.

11. “The Most Dangerous Game” by Richard Connell

Teach: Suspense

This is an especially accessible choice if you want students to analyze how an author creates suspense rather than simply identify that a story is suspenseful.

Students can examine pacing, conflict, setting, sensory details, and the information Connell reveals or withholds. Have them choose a particularly suspenseful passage and identify the specific techniques that make it work.

12. “The Cask of Amontillado” by Edgar Allan Poe

Teach: Dramatic Irony

Montresor tells readers very early that he intends to seek revenge against Fortunato. Fortunato, however, walks willingly toward his fate.

That difference in knowledge creates dramatic irony throughout the story. Students can analyze Montresor’s language and identify moments that have one meaning to Fortunato and another meaning to the reader.

It is also a strong choice for characterization and examining the reliability of a first-person narrator.

13. “The Black Cat” by Edgar Allan Poe

Teach: Unreliable Narrator

If your students enjoyed analyzing the narrator of “The Tell-Tale Heart,” “The Black Cat” provides an opportunity to push that skill further.

Students can examine the narrator’s attempts to explain and justify his actions and distinguish between what he claims about himself and what his behavior actually reveals.

For classroom use, preview the story because it contains violence toward both animals and people.

14. “The Veldt” by Ray Bradbury

Teach: Setting

The nursery in “The Veldt” is not simply where the story takes place. The setting drives the conflict.

Have students trace how Bradbury transforms the nursery from an impressive piece of technology into something increasingly threatening. Students can examine sensory imagery, repeated details, and changes in the setting to determine how the nursery contributes to characterization, conflict, and theme.

This is also an especially interesting story to revisit now because of its questions about technology, parenting, and dependence on devices.

15. “The Boarded Window” by Ambrose Bierce

Teach: Foreshadowing and Plot Twist

“The Boarded Window” is a good choice when you want students to see how a twist ending can change their understanding of everything that came before it.

After students finish reading, have them return to the beginning and look for clues Bierce planted throughout the story. Ask which details seemed insignificant during the first reading but become important after the ending.

16. “The Open Window” by Saki

Teach: Situational Irony

This one isn’t horror in the traditional sense, but its eerie setup makes it a fun October addition.

Students can examine how Vera controls both Framton’s expectations and the reader’s. The eventual reveal makes this particularly useful for teaching situational irony and discussing how authors deliberately manipulate audience expectations.

17. “The Pedestrian” by Ray Bradbury

Teach: Mood and Setting

A man walking alone at night doesn’t sound particularly frightening. Bradbury makes it frightening.

Students can examine how the deserted streets, empty houses, darkness, and technology create an increasingly eerie atmosphere. It’s a manageable text for helping students distinguish between setting and mood while analyzing the relationship between the two.

18. “Click-Clack the Rattlebag” by Neil Gaiman

Teach: Suspense and Pacing

This is a great example of how an author can create suspense without immediately revealing the threat.

Students can examine the information Gaiman withholds, how the characters move through the setting, and how the pacing changes as the story progresses. Ask students to identify exactly where they began to suspect something was wrong and what textual clues caused that reaction.

Because contemporary short fiction can have different reproduction/access restrictions than public-domain classics, make sure you’re using an authorized classroom copy.

19. “The Goophered Grapevine” by Charles W. Chesnutt

Teach: Frame Narrative and Folklore

For something different from traditional Gothic horror, consider Chesnutt’s use of conjure and folklore in “The Goophered Grapevine.”

The story-within-a-story structure gives students an opportunity to examine frame narrative and consider how the identity and motivations of a storyteller affect the story being told.

It can also lead to richer discussions about folklore, dialect, audience, and historical context.

20. “The Fall of the House of Usher” by Edgar Allan Poe

Teach: Gothic Setting

If you want to end your October reading with full Gothic atmosphere, this is hard to beat.

The decaying house, oppressive landscape, strange sounds, illness, isolation, and increasingly disturbing events allow students to identify characteristics of Gothic literature and analyze how setting can function almost like another character.

Have students track descriptions of the house alongside descriptions of Roderick Usher and consider why Poe draws so many parallels between them.
